title: The Capital Carried Downriver
summary: A displaced highland coalition and a newly founded capital meet through worker organization, changing trade routes, and layered imperial jurisdiction.
history: Highland households fleeing famine joined beneath a negotiator who secured refuge through protection agreements rather than claiming an empty landscape. In 591 a dynasty moved its court downriver and founded a new capital beside the main grain landing. Its ceremonies announced victory before walls and drains were complete. A performer portraying a workshop organizer helped laborers compare the unequal terms under which they built the city. An appointed governor then joined distant dependencies into one jurisdiction to redirect unofficial trade. The new center gained real commercial strength while straining older refuge agreements. Present descendants occupy a layered street where royal splendor, migrant survival, and ordinary collective bargaining cannot be cleanly separated.
question: whether capital households can revise assessments without extinguishing the finite protection agreements under which highland refugees first settled.
transformations: A performer’s roles as an organizer and a struggling mother become public drama connecting household survival with collective bargaining.
A dynasty relocating power and founding a victorious capital becomes court migration and an unfinished ceremonial city.
A refuge polity forming amid displacement and negotiated outside protection becomes a highland coalition with contested boundaries.
A late imperial jurisdiction reorganized around trade and security becomes a governor’s attempt to consolidate distant landing dependencies.
rows: Salla of the Raised Tally

Salla portrayed a worker holding an expense tally instead of a sword. Audiences copied the gesture at wage meetings. Patrons praised its dignity while requesting that performances avoid the contracts currently burdening their own workshops.
The Victorious Unfinished Street

Monuments along the street span successive courts, with drainage channels older than their inscriptions. Residents fund repairs beneath official triumphal arches. The street’s grandeur depends on household labor rarely included in histories of royal foundation.
The Highland Protection Houses

Refuge households shared guarantees across several clans rather than one uniform ancestry. Descendants disagree about outside patronage. Their surviving agreements protect named landings, not a timeless right of every patron to govern every later resident.
The Court’s Downriver Removal

Court migration shifted grain demand and witness fees toward a new capital. Old towns lost income while providing supplies. Royal chronicles call the move necessary unity; household records reveal a decision with benefits and costs distributed unevenly.
The Refuge Negotiator’s Cup

The cup authenticated several finite protection loans. Later rulers displayed it as submission to permanent rule. Its inscriptions specify seasons and named households, creating a material limit to the broader authority advertised through ceremonial custody.
The Expense Held Overhead

Workers display actual expense tallies during negotiations, borrowing Salla’s theatrical gesture. Officials forbid oversized boards. The protest’s force lies in quantities spectators can recognize, not in declaring every employer personally cruel.
The Governor’s Joined Dependencies

The jurisdiction lists distant places together without describing their different routes. Clerks apply one assessment to unequal journeys. Corrected route accounts expose why administrative unity cannot make every delivery cost the same amount of food and labor.
The Drain Arch Weaverbird

Birds nest beneath warm arches and carry fibers into drains. Builders once removed every nest ceremonially. Residents now preserve safe niches and clear channels selectively, separating useful maintenance from a spectacle that damages living neighbors unnecessarily.
The Famine Coalition Road

The road joins old refuge shelters now used by builders traveling to the capital. Protection payments still follow earlier boundaries. Revising them requires recognizing changed use without pretending the original refugee households never needed the guarantees.
The Protection Is Not Succession Clause

Outside protection does not convey permanent succession unless separately witnessed. Patron heirs seek to merge the two. The clause permits continued cooperation while challenging an inherited authority larger than any founding agreement actually granted.
Mosen of the Joined Refuge

Mosen negotiated among displaced households with incompatible traditions. Later histories describe one people following one founder. Supply lists show repeated disagreement and practical compromise, preserving a coalition’s achievement without inventing the uniformity it never possessed.
The Old Capital Storehouse

The court left a sound storehouse and several unpaid keepers behind. New claimants want its stone for monuments. Local kitchens propose continued grain use, connecting restoration to present need rather than either loyalty to the departed dynasty or decorative reuse.
The Capital Workshop Assembly

Builders compare wages and meal costs across contractors. Some skilled members exclude carriers from voting. A second tally campaign challenges that distinction, revealing inherited bargaining hierarchies inside a movement publicly celebrated for collective solidarity.
The First Royal Drain Failure

A festival crowd overwhelmed unfinished drains beneath the victorious street. Officials blamed migrant habits. Work orders show the system had never been completed, establishing an ordinary cause concealed by a politically convenient account of disorder.
The City Foundation Basket

The ceremonial basket once carried construction spoil. Its luxurious lining is later. Displaying both layers acknowledges the ordinary work beneath royal founding, though some patrons prefer an immaculate relic untouched by the history that made it significant.
The Refuge Meal Named

Hosts name both refugee contributions and local assistance during commemorative meals. The practice avoids portraying either group as passive. Disputes remain over unpaid loans, making acknowledgment a beginning of accounting rather than a substitute for it.
The Street in Four Courts

This manuscript follows one street through four jurisdictions and changing uses. It records residents between reigns. Readers can therefore distinguish a dynasty’s departure from the disappearance of people whose repairs and obligations continued beneath its renamed monuments.
The Foundation Basket’s Dust

Fine dust returns inside the basket after each unmet drain assessment. Most matches exposed mortar nearby, but a covered test repeats the deposit. Custodians respond by recording unfinished work, linking the uncertainty to a task they already know requires completion.
Capital Stone Reuse

Masons inspect old stone before recutting it. Reuse saves quarry labor but can erase inscriptions authenticating narrow rights. Workshop agreements require recording marks first, giving practical craft a role in preserving evidence without freezing every useful material permanently.
The Old Refuge Assessment

Refuge payments now burden households generations removed from arrival. Patron heirs offer no corresponding service. A hearing compares original scope and present benefit, asking whether protection can be renewed, substituted, or discharged without inventing consent from mere continuity.
